Plan for annual bills: a sinking fund with a calendar

Map four periodic expenses, follow the monthly reserve balance and see why a balanced annual budget can still run short before a bill arrives.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Hypothetical twelve-month calendar starting before month 1. Contributions arrive before the bill payment at each month-end. Four example bills fall in months 3, 6, 8 and 12. Starting reserve is already earmarked for these bills. No interest, inflation or other income and expenses are included. The central idea

The annual total tells you how much spending is planned. The calendar tells you when the cash must already be available.

01

Give predictable bills their own place in the plan

Some expenses arrive every month, while others arrive at particular points in the year. The Financial Consumer Agency of Canada’s budgeting lesson includes irregular and periodic expenses in the budget and describes spreading a known expense over the months before it is due.

A sinking fund is money earmarked over time for those planned payments. The label is less important than the amount, date and funding source. A future insurance renewal or booked trip can be planned separately from unexpected expenses whose timing and size are unknown.

This example lists four hypothetical bills: insurance in month three, maintenance in month six, travel in month eight, and gifts or events in month twelve. The chart’s fixed dates make the timing visible. Actual maintenance and event costs can differ, so use your own records and payment notices when building a real calendar.

02

An annual average can miss the first-year cash need

The default bills total CAD 4,500, equivalent to CAD 375 a month over a full year. The example also starts with CAD 500 already reserved. At a CAD 375 monthly contribution, the year ends with CAD 500 still earmarked.

However, after the month-eight travel bill, the projected balance is negative CAD 100. By that point, cumulative bills are CAD 3,600 while starting cash plus eight contributions totals CAD 3,500. A positive year-end amount does not pay a bill that falls before the later contributions arrive.

The signed monthly line exposes that timing gap. A negative point means the scheduled spending lacks funding within this reserve. It is not an approved overdraft or a prediction that a bank will permit the payment. Identify another source or revise the plan before the due date.

03

Solve for the contribution that covers each deadline

For every month m, compare cumulative bills due by that month with the starting reserve R. A constant monthly contribution C must satisfy R + Cm ≥ cumulative bills through month m. The smallest non-negative C is the largest value of (cumulative bills − R) ÷ m across the twelve months, floored at zero.

In the default calendar, month eight is the binding deadline. The required contribution is (CAD 3,600 − CAD 500) ÷ 8 = CAD 387.50. The comparison line uses that amount and avoids a negative month-end balance within the illustrated year.

This is a timing calculation, not an affordability assessment. The solved amount must still fit the operating budget after other spending and saving. A larger initial reserve, a revised bill amount or a different payment schedule can change the requirement; any actual schedule change needs agreement with the relevant provider.

04

Use all four graphics together

The bill bars identify the amounts and deadlines. The line chart follows the signed reserve after each month’s contribution and payment. The waterfall reconciles starting cash plus twelve contributions less all listed bills to the year-end balance.

The waterfall deliberately leaves the payment order out of its annual total. Use it to check arithmetic, then return to the monthly path to check availability. The matrix compares alternative starting reserves and monthly saving amounts, reporting the largest unfunded month-end balance in each case.

The example assumes contributions arrive before bills at month-end. If a payment is due earlier than the transfer, an end-of-month model may hide an intra-month shortage. Add actual paydays, transfer settlement times and bill deadlines to the detailed plan. No interest is earned here, so the results depend on cash timing rather than an investment forecast.

05

Keep the reserve and the budget consistent

A transfer between your own accounts changes where cash is held and how it is earmarked; it does not itself consume household wealth. When reviewing a consolidated budget, avoid treating both the transfer and the later bill as two separate purchases. The bill is the spending; the transfer prepares the cash for it.

Also avoid assigning the same opening reserve to several goals. If these dollars are committed to known annual bills, they are unavailable for another planned payment unless you replace the funding. Review the emergency reserve separately for genuinely unexpected costs.

After each payment, update the actual amount, remaining balance and next deadline. This is a one-year illustration; it does not automatically assume the same opening balance in every future year. Recalculate as prices, plans and bill dates change, and connect the transfer schedule with the income that funds it.
